text: Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters! And you who have no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money, without cost.
Why spend your silver on what is not bread, your labor on what does not satisfy? Listen carefully to me, and eat what is good; let your soul delight in the richest of fare.

versions.text: Why spend your silver on what is not bread, your labor on what does not satisfy? Listen to me, listen well, and you will eat what is good; you will delight in the richest of fare.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew uses imperatives ("eat what is good") and a jussive ("let your soul delight"), which the translation flattens into future statements. Restoring the invitational force also improves the rhythm of the call and avoids the slightly awkward doubling "Listen to me, listen well."

text: Turn your ear and come to me; listen, and you will live. I will make an everlasting covenant with you, my faithful mercies promised to David.
See, I made him a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander of the nations.
See, you will summon a nation you do not know, and a nation that does not know you will run to you, for the sake of the LORD your God, and of the Holy One of Israel, because he has glorified you.

versions.text: See, you will summon a nation you do not know, and a nation that does not know you will hasten to you, because of the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has two coordinated objects of לְמַעַן ("for the sake of the LORD your God, and for the Holy One of Israel"). The current rendering turns the second phrase into an appositive, losing the parallel structure of the line.

versions.text: See, you will summon a nation you do not know, and a nation that does not know you will hasten to you, because of the LORD your God, and for the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you.
versions.explanation: The revision rightly restored the two coordinated objects of לְמַעַן, but the English now pairs unlike prepositions ("because of ... and for ..."), which blurs the parallel it was meant to recover, and it stacks a third "for" at the head of the causal clause. Matching the two objects under one preposition ("for the sake of ... and of ...") and using "because" for כִּי keeps the parallelism audible when read aloud. "Run" also renders יָרוּצוּ more concretely than the flatter "hasten."

text: Seek the LORD while he may be found; call on him while he is near.
Let the wicked forsake his way and the evildoer his thoughts. Let him return to the LORD, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he will freely pardon.
For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways, declares the LORD.
As the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways and my thoughts than your thoughts.
As the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there without watering the earth, making it bud and flourish, so that it yields seed for the sower and bread for the eater,
so is my word that goes out from my mouth: it will not return to me empty, but will accomplish what I desire and achieve the purpose for which I sent it.
You will go out with joy and be led forth in peace; the mountains and hills will break into song before you, and all the trees of the field will clap their hands.
Instead of the thornbush the cypress will rise, and instead of briers the myrtle will grow. This will bring renown to the LORD, an everlasting sign that will never be cut off.

versions.text: Instead of the thornbush the cypress will rise, and instead of briers the myrtle will grow. This will be a memorial to the LORD, an everlasting sign that will never be destroyed.
versions.explanation: לְשֵׁם means "for a name/renown," not "a memorial," which suggests a monument to the dead. Also יִכָּרֵת means "be cut off," fitting the plant imagery of the verse better than "destroyed."
